_comment: Single source for urgent-care guidance and crisis lines (Phase 1 safety, 26 Oct 2026). Rendered on /urgent/, /support/, the Profile and the footer; the Ask worker carries a copy of the crisis lines that tools/ask_core_test.mjs checks against this file. Re-verify every entry at least every 3 months (verifyBy).

urgent.title: When to get help quickly
urgent.intro: Most tinnitus is not a sign of anything dangerous. A few situations need medical attention quickly. This page explains which ones, calmly and without guesswork.

tiers.label: Get emergency help now
tiers.lead: Call your emergency number or go to an emergency department if tinnitus comes with:
items: sudden weakness or drooping of the face, arm or leg, numbness, trouble speaking or seeing, a sudden severe headache, or other sudden changes in how your body works. These can be signs of a stroke.
pulsing tinnitus together with new head or neck pain, especially after a neck injury or neck manipulation. This can be a sign of a torn artery in the neck.
sudden, severe spinning dizziness (vertigo) that does not settle.

tiers.label: Get medical help today
tiers.lead: Contact a doctor the same day if:
items: your hearing has suddenly dropped or sounds muffled in one or both ears, even if it started days or a few weeks ago. Treatment works best when started early. If you cannot be seen today, go to an emergency department or urgent care.
you have new tinnitus that beats in time with your pulse and came on suddenly.
you have ear pain with fluid coming from the ear, swelling around the ear or a high temperature, or earache that has lasted more than 2 to 3 days.

tiers.label: Book an appointment soon
tiers.lead: Arrange a non-urgent appointment with your doctor or an audiologist if:
items: you hear tinnitus in one ear only and it does not go away.
you have pulsing tinnitus that has been there for a while. The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment for this.
your hearing is getting worse over weeks, or is clearly different between your ears.
you keep getting earache, or dizziness that keeps coming back.
tinnitus is affecting your sleep, mood, concentration or daily life.

urgent.crisisLine: If you are thinking about suicide, or feel you cannot cope, you can talk to someone now. If you are in immediate danger, call your emergency number.

basis.label: NHS: Tinnitus (reviewed 12 Jan 2024; checked 26 Oct 2026): go to A&E or call 999 for tinnitus after a head injury, or with sudden hearing loss, facial weakness or vertigo; urgent GP appointment for tinnitus that beats with your pulse
NHS: Hearing loss (reviewed 30 May 2025): urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for sudden hearing loss

NICE NG155 (2020), recommendations 1.2.1 to 1.2.7, checked against nice.org.uk on 26 Oct 2026: refer immediately to a crisis mental health team for tinnitus with a high risk of suicide; refer immediately for sudden-onset significant neurological symptoms or signs, acute uncontrolled vertigo or suspected stroke; within 24 hours for hearing loss that developed suddenly (over 3 days or less) in the past 30 days; within 2 weeks for distress affecting mental wellbeing, or hearing loss that is rapidly worsening; consider referral for persistent pulsatile or one-sided tinnitus
Ellis et al., British Journal of General Practice 2022: sudden-onset pulsatile tinnitus warrants emergency assessment

NHS: Earache (reviewed 27 Oct 2025): urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for earache lasting more than 2 to 3 days, fluid from the ear, swelling around the ear, a very high temperature or a change in hearing
NIDCD: Sudden deafness (updated 14 Sep 2018): treat as a medical emergency; treatment delayed more than two to four weeks is less likely to help
RNID: Sudden hearing loss (updated 27 May 2026): can be a medical emergency; contact NHS 111 or your GP, or go to A&E if you cannot
CDC: Signs and Symptoms of Stroke (page dated 19 May 2026): call 911 right away for any sudden sign of stroke, including a severe headache with no known cause

Keser, Meschia and Lanzino, Mayo Clinic Proceedings 2022 (PMID 35379423), and Pacheco-López et al., Journal of Clinical Medicine 2025 (PMID 40648801) (both reviewed for Tinnitus Claims Check, Oct 2026): pulsatile tinnitus with head or neck pain can signal a torn neck artery, which needs emergency assessment

AAO-HNSF Clinical Practice Guideline: Tinnitus Update (Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery, Oct 2026; doi 10.1002/ohn.70417): clinicians should ask about self-harm risk (KAS 3) and obtain a comprehensive audiological evaluation (KAS 5)

crisis.title: Crisis support
crisis.intro: If you are thinking about suicide, or feel you cannot keep yourself safe, please talk to someone now. These services are free and confidential, and staffed by trained people.

services.name: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
services.contact: Call or text 988, or chat online

services.name: Text 50808
services.note: Verified on the HSE (Irish health service) page; the service's own site was unavailable when checked

directory.name: Find A Helpline
directory.contact: Free helplines in more than 175 countries
directory.note: Run by ThroughLine; helplines verify their details directly

crisis.danger: If you are in immediate danger, call your local emergency number.
crisis.limits: Tinnitus Evidence is an information website. It cannot provide counselling, does not monitor messages, and cannot follow up with anyone.

organizations.name: Tinnitus UK
organizations.offers: Free helpline 0800 018 0527 (Monday to Friday, 10am to 4pm UK time), webchat, text and email (details on their website), support groups and a free online course

organizations.name: American Tinnitus Association
organizations.offers: Information line 800-634-8978, support-group directory and peer volunteers

organizations.name: Chime: tinnitus support
organizations.offers: Information and one-to-one support for people with tinnitus

organizations.name: Deutsche Tinnitus-Liga
organizations.offers: Peer advice line and self-help groups (in German)

organizations.offers: Listening and information line 1-877-276-7772, in French and English
